system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 7 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old man with a history of alcoholic cirrhosis and severe asthma was admitted after developing hypercarbic respiratory failure during an asthma exacerbation, requiring intubation and mechanical ventilation. He was transferred to the ICU, where he was treated with sedation, paralysis, and antibiotics after bronchoscopy revealed influenza B, MSSA, and Serratia. He improved clinically, was successfully extubated, and transitioned to oral therapy. Imaging showed cirrhosis and a liver lesion requiring further evaluation with MRI. His home medications for cirrhosis and asthma were restarted. He was discharged to an extended care facility for rehabilitation with follow-up arranged for hepatology, pulmonology, and consideration of Xolair and sleep apnea evaluation.

conversation_lines.text: I understand. But those follow-ups are important, especially with your history. We’ll get things back on track. For now, your breathing is better since the nebs and steroids in the ER. Your peak flow improved from 160 to 250.

conversation_lines.text: That’s good. But my stomach still hurts. I even had a couple shots of alcohol the night before to numb it—haven’t had a drink in nine months, but I couldn’t take it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Alcohol can make your liver and stomach issues worse. We’ll need to check your abdomen. A CT scan was done today—no sign of pancreatitis, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s causing the pain then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not sure yet. Your liver enzymes and alkaline phosphatase are elevated. We’ll do an ultrasound tomorrow to look at your liver and bile ducts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. ___, the ultrasound showed your liver looks cirrhotic, as expected, but no mass. Your bile ducts are normal, and no ascites. But your alkaline phosphatase is still high. We’re still concerned about the abdominal pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve consulted GI. They recommend an EGD—upper endoscopy—to look at your esophagus and stomach. Given your pain and history, it might show something we can treat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: An endoscopy? That sounds rough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s very safe. You’ll be sedated. It helps us see if there’s an ulcer, infection, or inflammation causing your pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. ___, the EGD is done. You had candida—yeast—in your esophagus, which can happen with inhaled steroids. We’re starting fluconazole for that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeast? In my throat?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, candidal esophagitis. It can cause pain when swallowing. We also found ulcers in your stomach. The biopsy showed cytomegalovirus—CMV—causing the ulcers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: CMV? Isn’t that something you get from…?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a common virus, but in people with weakened immunity—like from cirrhosis or long-term steroids—it can reactivate and cause ulcers. We’re starting valganciclovir to treat it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that fix the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It should help. We’re also increasing your omeprazole to reduce stomach acid and help the ulcers heal. You’ll need another EGD in eight weeks to check progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your CMV viral load came back—no virus detected in the blood. That’s good. It means the infection might be localized to the stomach, not spreading.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m not contagious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, not at all. But we’re still treating it to heal the ulcers. Also, we’re starting Bactrim to prevent another infection called PJP, which you’re at risk for.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: More pills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know it’s a lot. But they’re important. We’re also watching your vision—CMV can affect the eyes. If you notice blurry vision, tell us right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an MRCP today—a special MRI of your liver and bile ducts. It showed cirrhosis, as expected. But there are some nodules in your liver—about 6 cm across.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A mass? Is it cancer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not clear yet. The appearance isn’t classic for cancer. It could be dysplastic nodules—pre-cancerous changes from cirrhosis. But we need to be sure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what happens now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll follow up with Dr. ___ in hepatology. They’ll likely do a biopsy to rule out cancer. You’ll call their office tomorrow to schedule it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been avoiding doctors… but I guess I can’t anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I get it. But catching things early makes a big difference. This way, we can treat it before it becomes serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your breathing has improved. Peak flow is now 390. We’re stopping IV steroids and switching to a five-day prednisone burst. Keep using your inhalers as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been using them a lot. Is that bad?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It shows your asthma is active. But long-term steroid use can cause issues like the yeast infection. Use a spacer with your inhaler—it reduces the risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t know that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll get you one before discharge. Also, your pulmonologist will check your lung function with PFTs. Given your history, they might consider omalizumab—a stronger treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s the day we discharge you. Your breathing is stable, and your pain is better with oral Dilaudid. We’re sending you home with several new medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m going home? But what about the liver thing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The liver nodule needs outpatient follow-up. You’ll call Dr. ___ tomorrow. They’ll arrange the biopsy. It’s urgent, so please don’t delay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. What about the pills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll take fluconazole for three weeks, valganciclovir twice daily, and Bactrim three times a week. Also, omeprazole twice daily, and keep using your asthma meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the painkillers?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Only Dilaudid as needed, every four hours. We’re cutting back to avoid dependence. Please follow your PCP’s plan to eventually stop them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want to be on them forever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And please keep all your follow-ups—liver, lung, and primary care. They’re key to staying out of the hospital.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. I promise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s all we ask. You’ve made good progress. Take care of yourself, and call if anything worsens—especially trouble breathing or severe pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I really appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Get some rest, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—should I stop drinking for good?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. With cirrhosis, any alcohol can accelerate liver damage. Staying sober is one of the best things you can do for your health.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t had a drink in nine months. I’ll keep it that way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent. Keep it up. You’re on the right path.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the weight gain? I’ve put on 60 pounds in a year.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That can worsen asthma and liver disease. Work with your PCP on diet and safe exercise. Even small changes help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll start today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the spirit. You’ve got this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again. I feel better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Glad to hear it. Take your meds, rest, and call us if you need anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you at follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Looking forward to it. Take care, Mr. ___.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old man with a history of alcoholic cirrhosis, severe asthma, and chronic abdominal pain was admitted for an asthma exacerbation and worsening epigastric pain. He had not followed up with specialists after a recent intubation for asthma. Initial management included bronchodilators and steroids for asthma. Abdominal pain persisted despite normal CT and ultrasound; an EGD revealed candidal esophagitis and CMV-positive gastric ulcers, leading to treatment with fluconazole and valganciclovir. An MRCP showed cirrhosis and a 6.2 cm liver nodule concerning for dysplastic changes or early malignancy, necessitating outpatient hepatology follow-up for biopsy. Asthma improved with therapy, and he was discharged home on multiple new medications with plans for pulmonology, ID, and GI follow-up. He committed to sobriety and adherence to care.
